title: Quiz: Scaling, Encoding, and the recipes Pipeline

questions.text: After Z-score standardisation, a variable has a mean of 42,000 and an original value of 70,000 with standard deviation 28,000. What is the standardised value?
questions.explanation: Z = (70,000 − 42,000) / 28,000 = 28,000 / 28,000 = 1.0. The value is exactly one standard deviation above the mean.

questions.text: Min-Max scaling maps all values to [0, 1]. What is its main weakness compared to Z-score standardisation?
options: It changes the mean of the distribution
It is sensitive to outliers — one extreme value compresses all other values into a narrow band
It requires the variable to be normally distributed first
It cannot be applied to variables with a minimum value of zero
questions.explanation: Min-Max scaling divides by (max − min). If one outlier makes max very large, all genuine values get compressed into a narrow range near 0. Z-score standardisation is less affected because a single outlier has less relative impact on the standard deviation.

questions.text: A categorical variable has 5 levels. How many binary dummy columns should you create to encode it without perfect multicollinearity?
options: Depends on the number of observations
questions.explanation: For k categories, you create k − 1 dummy variables. The dropped category becomes the reference level (all zeros). This avoids perfect multicollinearity (the dummy variable trap). For 5 levels: 5 − 1 = 4 columns.

questions.text: You apply step_normalize() before step_dummy() in a recipe. What problem does this cause?
options: Normalisation fails because character columns are present
The dummy variables (which will be created later) cannot be normalised
No problem — step order does not matter in recipes
It causes the recipe to skip the dummy encoding step
questions.explanation: step_normalize() applied to all numeric predictors will fail if nominal (character/factor) columns are still present in the dataset — they cannot be standardised. Always encode (step_dummy) before scaling (step_normalize). The correct order is: impute → dummy → normalise.

questions.text: In a recipes pipeline, prep() should be called on the FULL dataset (including the test set) to ensure the scaling statistics are accurate.
questions.explanation: prep() must be called on the TRAINING set only. Using the test set in prep() would let test-set statistics influence the scaling parameters — a form of data leakage that makes your evaluation overly optimistic.

questions.text: You want to encode education (None < Primary < Secondary < Tertiary < Postgraduate) as a predictor. Which encoding is most appropriate?
options: Ordinal encoding (1, 2, 3, 4, 5) because the categories have a natural order
Target encoding using the mean outcome per level
Frequency encoding using the count of each level
questions.explanation: Education has a clear ordinal structure, so mapping it to integers 1–5 preserves that ordering and uses a single column instead of 4 dummy columns. One-hot encoding would discard the ordering information.
